questions.stem_html: Respiratory epithelial cells from a pig are simultaneously infected by two influenza A viruses. One virus has a hemagglutinin adapted to human receptors, and the other contains several internal gene segments derived from an avian strain. Progeny virions are isolated that contain the human-adapted hemagglutinin segment together with avian-derived internal segments. Which process produced these progeny?

options.text_html: Reassortment of separate viral RNA genome segments during coinfection
Gradual accumulation of point mutations during serial transmission
Integration of a DNA intermediate into the host-cell genome
Homologous recombination between two nonsegmented positive-sense RNA genomes
Transfer of viral genes by a bacteriophage particle

questions.explanation_html: Influenza A has a segmented negative-sense RNA genome. When two strains infect the same cell, newly assembled virions can package genome segments derived from both parental viruses. This reassortment can create an abrupt major antigenic change, termed antigenic shift, and may generate a virus with a novel combination of surface and internal proteins.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Point mutations in hemagglutinin or neuraminidase produce antigenic drift, a gradual process rather than wholesale exchange of segments.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Influenza replicates without a DNA intermediate and does not require integration into the host genome.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The key event in this scenario is exchange of intact segmented genomes, not homologous recombination between nonsegmented genomes.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Bacteriophages infect bacteria and do not mediate gene exchange between influenza virions.

questions.educational_objective: Coinfection by distinct influenza A strains permits reassortment of the virus's segmented RNA genome, producing abrupt antigenic shift and novel combinations of viral proteins.
